title: I saw agentic trading coming in 2023. Here’s what I’m predicting next.
author: NextgenAITrading
selftext:
When I started, the LLM was basically an interface. You described a trading idea, and it configured the rules and spit out a backtest. I still had to drive the research myself.

Today, I can start with a vague idea and have agents research it, build strategies, backtest them, optimize them, and deploy with my permission. I’ve used this workflow across two real-money public portfolio challenges.

**My prediction:** we have roughly five years of abundant opportunity before these workflows become commonplace.

Then the edge shifts toward data. If everyone’s agents use the same prices, fundamentals, and indicators, they’ll keep discovering and competing over the same trades.

That’s why I intend to train my own LLM using the backtesting corpus and agent conversations I’ve collected building NexusTrade, alongside reinforcement learning.

[Full article with screenshots, public portfolios, and open-source runbooks](https://nexustrade.io/blog/agentic-trading-next-five-years-20261009).

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Training on the NexusTrade backtesting corpus and agent conversations could encode useful research habits, but it could also teach the model to reproduce the selection process that produced the two public portfolio challenges. How will you split the corpus so later prompts, optimization attempts, and performance feedback cannot leak into evaluation? A convincing RL test would lock an unseen time period and strategy family, then measure whether the agent generates robust candidates with fewer trials, not just higher best-run returns. The attached image appears illustrative; I cannot read portfolio statistics from it.

replies.author: NextgenAITrading
replies.body:
The corpus is broader than the two portfolio challenges. It includes 222,010 backtests and years of strategy experiments and agent conversations. The portfolios are examples of how I'm using the current workflow.

But the leakage issue you raised applies to that whole corpus. I'd keep each research chain together, including later prompts, parameter searches, failed attempts and performance feedback. Related strategy variations would stay in the same split too.

I'd then hold out a strategy family and time period, freeze the model, and compare it with the baseline using the same tools and trial budget. I agree that finding strategies that hold up after costs with fewer attempts would be a more useful result than reporting the best backtest it produced.

That evaluation design still needs work. The article describes what I intend to train, and I haven't laid out a complete RL protocol there. I'd also want a forward test, since excluding a historical period from my dataset doesn't mean the base model hasn't seen information about it.

The article has the portfolio figures and direct links to both accounts if you want to inspect them. The Reddit preview image doesn't show those details.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The point that the edge shifts to data once everyone's agents use the same prices and indicators is the one I agree with most. Two caveats on the five-year window: it's hard to tell skill from luck in a few public portfolio challenges, so the useful evidence is a long record against a benchmark with the trial count, and training on your own backtesting corpus can bake in the survivorship of the strategies that were saved. Structured, timestamped event data (earnings, macro releases, corporate actions) is the kind of non-price input that could differentiate agents, and Cymetica's EventTrader is one example of it.
